summary: Moses ben Jacob Cordovero (1522-1570), known by the acronym the Ramak, was the leading systematizer of kabbalah in sixteenth-century Safed in the generation before Isaac Luria. His Pardes Rimonim ('Orchard of Pomegranates') is a systematic summa of pre-Lurianic kabbalah, and his Tomer Devorah ('The Palm Tree of Deborah') is an ethical-mystical work on imitatio Dei through the sefirot, in particular on emulating the thirteen attributes of divine mercy. He was the brother-in-law of Solomon Alkabetz and a teacher whose synthesis Luria's later system partly superseded.
description:
Moses ben Jacob Cordovero, known by the acronym the Ramak (Rabbi Moshe Cordovero), lived in Safed (Tzfat) in the Galilee, the sixteenth-century centre of kabbalistic activity gathered around figures such as Joseph Karo and Solomon Alkabetz. He is recorded in the tradition as the great systematizer of kabbalah in the generation before Isaac Luria (the Arizal). He was a student and brother-in-law of Solomon Alkabetz, and himself the teacher of many of the Safed kabbalists, including, in the accounts, the young Luria. He died in Safed in 1570.

Cordovero's major theoretical work is the Pardes Rimonim ('Orchard of Pomegranates'), which the tradition and modern scholarship alike treat as the first comprehensive and orderly synthesis of the kabbalah that had developed since the Zohar, a systematic summa organized by topic (the gates, or she'arim) that gathers, harmonizes, and analyzes the doctrines of the sefirot, the divine names, and the structure of the emanated worlds. It became a standard reference for the study of theoretical kabbalah. His work of ethical-mystical instruction is the Tomer Devorah ('The Palm Tree of Deborah', a short treatise later printed at Venice in 1588), which sets out a programme of imitatio Dei: the human being is to resemble the Creator by emulating the divine qualities as they are configured in the sefirot. Its first chapter opens, in the open text on Sefaria, 'It is fitting for a person to resemble his Creator, and then he will be in the secret of the Highest Form, in image and likeness', and expounds the thirteen supernal attributes of mercy (read by the tradition out of Micah 7:18-20, rendered in the Sefaria text as 'Who is a power like You, who bears iniquity and passes over transgression') as thirteen traits a person is to practise toward others: tolerance of insult, bearing the wrongs of one's fellow, pardon, and the rest, so that (in the chapter's closing words) 'just as a person acts below, so too will he merit to open for himself the highest trait above'. This entry reports this teaching as Cordovero's own, set out in his text, and attributes it to him rather than affirming its metaphysics.

Cordovero's systematization is generally described in scholarship as the high point of the theosophical kabbalah that preceded Isaac Luria. Luria arrived in Safed near the end of Cordovero's life and, in the accounts, was briefly among those associated with him; the new and highly influential system Luria then taught, with its distinctive doctrines of the contraction (tzimtzum), the shattering of the vessels (shevirat ha-kelim), and cosmic repair (tikkun), reframed and in large measure superseded Cordovero's synthesis in the later reception of kabbalah, though Cordoveran and Lurianic ideas continued to be studied together (later kabbalists and Hasidic authors, Shneur Zalman of Liady among them, cite both Cordovero's Pardes and 'the Kabbalah of the Arizal' side by side). This entry states the relation between the two systems as the tradition and scholarship describe it, without ranking their truth.

Cordovero belonged to the Safed circle, the concentration of kabbalists and halakhists in the Galilean town, and this entry records him on the tradition's own terms as the systematizer of the Pardes Rimonim and the author of the Tomer Devorah, with his teaching attributed to him and his place before Luria stated as the tradition and scholarship report it.
